Anyone with common sense knows that while AI is undoubtedly helpful and can make computer scientists more efficient, we are nowhere near a point where it can replace them entirely.

2. It strengthens their position in salary negotiations with highly skilled workers. If workers feel uncertain about the market, they may be less likely to leave for other opportunities.

You can already program by just prompting and letting the AI do all the work, but here's the kicker. What are you going to do when you run into a bug in all those tens of thousands of lines of code and the AI can't fix it? You then have a problem, because then you will have to look for that bug like it's a needle in a haystack.

I don't see this as a realistic way of programming just quite yet. Right now AI is still just a helpful tool that makes programmers more productive, but it doesn't replace programmers. Not quite yet.

Not to mention all the stress of the complexity of all that code that the AI has generated when a bug pops up that AI can't fix. No, a programmer has to understand the code or he won't be able to work with it if things go wrong. As a programmer you have to know the code you're working on or you're going to have a problem and lots of stress.

comments.text:
Nerds and cool guys often have different perspectives, but both play a crucial role in discussions like these. Nerds tend to dive deep into details, analyzing technological advancements with precision. Cool guys, on the other hand, focus more on broader societal impacts and pragmatic aspects. Both perspectives are valuable—the question of who has deeper access to truth is complex.

Historically, nerds have often driven groundbreaking innovations through their meticulous approach to science and technology. However, cool guys have shaped real-world change by recognizing how to integrate these innovations into society. Take the rise of the internet, for example: while tech pioneers (the nerds) built the infrastructure, visionaries like Steve Jobs (the “cool guy”) understood how to bring it to the masses and transform the world.

But here’s why this is truly a non-decidable problem:
Sometimes, people watch a video titled “It’s all a bubble” and assume the creator is talking about AI. But then they realize the video was actually about how scientists often inflate the perceived value of their papers to secure funding, even when the real substance isn’t as groundbreaking as advertised. This means that the viewer unknowingly applied their own neurological (statistical) next-token prediction to complete the missing context.

Now, apply this to AGI: What if the final missing “ingredient” isn’t anything mystical, but rather just exposing AI to real-world robotics so it can form actual experiences? But what if, instead, consciousness itself is the key missing component? We simply don’t know—and that’s precisely why this debate remains undecidable.

At the end of the day, the most important thing is to keep questioning and exploring—because the real answer might be something neither nerds nor cool guys expect.

The AI only works with known data and whatever human data is available.

comments.text:
In short, you have to practice coding to understand abstractions, comprehend books, and interpret AI output. A detailed explanation follows.

The statement "Coding is Dead" is clickbait and a buzzword, similar to saying "Running is Dead; we have cars and motorcycles." The "Coding is Dead" statement is usually interpreted as "You do not have to spend time coding anymore," but this is a false assertion. The claim that "AI Will Replace Coders in 2025" is another example of a provocative statement. Since the era of frameworks, there have not been coders in the traditional sense for the past 10-20 years, as much of the coding work has been encapsulated within framework methods. However, coding as a practice is still very much alive, and I will explain here: coding is like a gym for an engineer.

You still need to read code, even if it is written by someone else. You need to understand concepts like variables, arrays, loops, objects, and so on. You should also understand algorithms, the reasons for bugs, and the places where bugs can occur. Thus, you still need to practice coding just as you practice lifting weights; otherwise, you will lack the mental capacity to understand the output of AI, just as you would lack the strength to use large kettlebells without practice.

The same analogy can be found right here: I am not a native English speaker, and I first write in English as I write, then I ask ChatGPT to fix spelling and grammar. Sometimes the output is brilliant; other times, I have to change plural forms or transform the output to adjust the mental accents of the entire sentence. I need to know English to get the full potential of ChatGPT, and I have to spend years practicing: extending my vocabulary, learning grammar, and just hanging around on English-speaking YouTube to be able to communicate with ChatGPT at an appropriate level, to feel that it has captured my thoughts correctly and added all the flavors and shades of my meanings.

Can I say that "Writing in English is Dead" just because I have translators and ChatGPT? Of course not. ChatGPT helps significantly, but the foundation you have to build yourself. The same goes for coding.

How can you explain what a class, an object, or an interface is in programming languages to someone who has not coded much? It is simply impossible. To understand these abstractions, one needs to have skills in procedural programming and experience with some issues that object-oriented programming solves well.

Summary: Software engineers must practice coding on a daily basis, just as police officers or firefighters must engage in physical training. Moreover, to be a good software engineer, one also needs to practice physical activities.

Without coding skills, it is impossible to read books about Operating System Architecture. Coding is like basic Algebra—an essential skill that is inevitably required.
